title: Chemical Equilibrium - Chemistry - Le Chatelier's Principle
subject: Chemistry

questions.q: Le Chatelier's Principle states that if a stress is applied to a system at equilibrium, the system will shift to:
questions.explain: Le Chatelier's Principle states that a system at equilibrium will respond to a disturbance (stress) by shifting its position in a direction that tends to counteract the disturbance.
questions.subject: Chemistry

questions.q: Consider the reaction: $\text{N}_2(g) + 3\text{H}_2(g) \rightleftharpoons 2\text{NH}_3(g)$ ($\Delta H < 0$). What is the effect of **increasing the temperature**?
questions.explain: The reaction is exothermic ($\Delta H < 0$), so heat is a product. Adding heat (increasing T) shifts equilibrium to the left (reactants) to consume the heat, and the value of the equilibrium constant $K​$ decreases.
questions.subject: Chemistry

questions.q: For the reaction $2\text{NO}_2(g) \rightleftharpoons \text{N}_2\text{O}_4(g)$, what happens if the **pressure is increased** by reducing the volume?
options: The equilibrium shifts to the left (more moles of gas).
The equilibrium shifts to the right (fewer moles of gas).
Both forward and reverse rates decrease.
questions.explain: Increasing pressure favors the side with fewer moles of gas. Reactants: 2 moles. Products: 1 mole. The system shifts right ($2 \rightarrow 1$) to reduce pressure.
questions.subject: Chemistry

questions.q: What is the effect of adding a **catalyst** to a reversible reaction at equilibrium?
options: It shifts the equilibrium to the right.
It shifts the equilibrium to the left.
It has no effect on the equilibrium position.
questions.explain: A catalyst increases the rates of both forward and reverse reactions equally by lowering activation energy. It speeds up the attainment of equilibrium but does not change the position of equilibrium or $K​$.
questions.subject: Chemistry

questions.q: In the reaction $\text{PCl}_5(g) \rightleftharpoons \text{PCl}_3(g) + \text{Cl}_2(g)$, adding **Inert Gas (e.g., Helium)** at constant **volume** will:
options: Shift the equilibrium to the right.
Shift the equilibrium to the left.
Have no effect on the equilibrium position.
questions.explain: Adding an inert gas at constant volume increases total pressure but does not change the partial pressures of the reacting species. Therefore, the equilibrium position remains unchanged.
questions.subject: Chemistry

questions.q: In the reaction $\text{PCl}_5(g) \rightleftharpoons \text{PCl}_3(g) + \text{Cl}_2(g)$, adding **Inert Gas (e.g., Helium)** at constant **pressure** (e.g., in a piston) will:
options: Shift the equilibrium to the side with more moles of gas (Right).
Shift the equilibrium to the side with fewer moles of gas (Left).
questions.explain: Adding inert gas at constant pressure increases volume, which decreases the partial pressures of all reacting species. The system shifts to the side with more moles of gas (the right) to restore pressure.
questions.subject: Chemistry

questions.q: Consider: $\text{CO}(g) + 2\text{H}_2(g) \rightleftharpoons \text{CH}_3\text{OH}(g)$. If **$\text{H}_2$ is removed** from the system:
options: The reaction shifts right to consume $\text{H}_2$.
The reaction shifts left to produce more $\text{H}_2$.
questions.explain: Removing a reactant creates a 'hole' that the system tries to fill. The equilibrium shifts to the left (reverse direction) to produce more $\text{H}_2$.
questions.subject: Chemistry

questions.q: For the endothermic reaction $\text{N}_2\text{O}_4(g) \rightleftharpoons 2\text{NO}_2(g)$ ($\Delta H > 0$), observing the mixture changes the color from colorless ($\text{N}_2\text{O}_4$) to brown ($\text{NO}_2$). What happens if you place the flask in **ice water**?
questions.explain: Since the reaction is endothermic (Heat + Reactant $\rightleftharpoons$ Product), removing heat (cooling) shifts the equilibrium to the left. The concentration of $\text{NO}_2$ (brown) decreases, and $\text{N}_2\text{O}_4$ (colorless) increases, making the mixture lighter.
questions.subject: Chemistry

questions.q: Which of the following changes will change the value of the equilibrium constant $K​$?
questions.explain: The equilibrium constant $K​$ is a function of temperature only. Changes in concentration, pressure, or volume shift the position of equilibrium but do not change the numerical value of $K​$.
questions.subject: Chemistry

questions.q: Given: $\text{C}(s) + \text{CO}_2(g) \rightleftharpoons 2\text{CO}(g)$. Adding more solid carbon $\text{C}(s)$ will:
options: Have no effect on the equilibrium position.
questions.explain: Solids have a constant activity of 1. Adding more solid does not change its concentration in a way that affects the equilibrium expression or position, provided some solid is present.
questions.subject: Chemistry

questions.q: In the Haber process $\text{N}_2(g) + 3\text{H}_2(g) \rightleftharpoons 2\text{NH}_3(g)$ (Exothermic), which set of conditions favors the **maximum yield** of ammonia?
questions.explain: Exothermic: Low Temp favors products (shift right). Mole decrease ($4 \rightarrow 2$): High Pressure favors products (shift right). Note: In industry, a moderate temp is used for rate reasons, but theoretically, low temp gives higher yield.
questions.subject: Chemistry

questions.q: For the reaction $H_2(g) + I_2(g) \rightleftharpoons 2HI(g)$, increasing the total pressure by decreasing volume will:
options: Have no effect on the equilibrium position.
questions.explain: Reactants have 2 moles of gas; Products have 2 moles of gas ($ \Delta n_g = 0 $). Pressure changes do not favor either side when mole numbers are equal.
questions.subject: Chemistry

questions.q: Consider the solubility equilibrium: $\text{AgCl}(s) \rightleftharpoons \text{Ag}^+(aq) + \text{Cl}^-(aq)$. Adding NaCl to the solution will:
questions.explain: This is the **Common Ion Effect**. Adding NaCl increases $[\text{Cl}^-]$. Le Chatelier's principle dictates the system shifts left to consume excess $\text{Cl}^-$, causing AgCl to precipitate and decreasing its solubility.
questions.subject: Chemistry

questions.q: Blood pH is maintained by the buffer system: $\text{H}^+(aq) + \text{HCO}_3^-(aq) \rightleftharpoons \text{H}_2\text{CO}_3(aq) \rightleftharpoons \text{H}_2\text{O}(l) + \text{CO}_2(g)$. Hyperventilation (exhaling too much $\text{CO}_2$) causes:
questions.explain: Removing $\text{CO}_2$ (product) pulls the equilibrium to the right (towards gas). Wait, looking at the full chain: $\text{H}^+ + \text{HCO}_3^- \rightarrow \text{CO}_2$. If $\text{CO}_2$ is lost, the reaction shifts to produce more $\text{CO}_2$, consuming $\text{H}^+$. Lower $\text{H}^+$ means higher pH (Alkalosis).
questions.subject: Chemistry

questions.q: Which factor changes the **rate** at which equilibrium is achieved but not the equilibrium **concentrations**?
questions.explain: A catalyst lowers the activation energy for both forward and reverse reactions, speeding up the approach to equilibrium without altering the thermodynamic equilibrium state ($K​$).
questions.subject: Chemistry

questions.q: In the reaction $\text{Fe}^{3+}(aq) + \text{SCN}^-(aq) \rightleftharpoons [\text{Fe(SCN)}]^{2+}(aq)$ (Deep Red). If $\text{Fe}^{3+}$ is added:
questions.explain: Adding reactant $\text{Fe}^{3+}$ shifts the equilibrium to the right to produce more product $[\text{Fe(SCN)}]^{2+}$, which is deep red.
questions.subject: Chemistry

questions.q: Consider the following reaction at equilibrium in a closed rigid container: $\text{CaCO}_3(s) \rightleftharpoons \text{CaO}(s) + \text{CO}_2(g)$. What is the effect of adding more $\text{CO}_2$ gas?
questions.explain: Adding product $\text{CO}_2$ shifts the equilibrium to the left to consume the excess gas, resulting in the formation of more solid reactant $\text{CaCO}_3$.
questions.subject: Chemistry
